p: Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you. I get the same issues, same issues, different agencies, different criteria, etcetera.

It's helpful. Thank you both. I will try to go faster because I think I've got a lot of questions still. So I’m sorry, Blame Molly. The– I understand that MOCS spends about

$10 million a year to maintain Passport. Could you break down how that funding is spent between Accenture and Avalua and what each of those entities does to support Passport?

Thank you for the question, Chair. I'll give it a shot. So I'll start with Ivalua. Ivalua provides the software that– for Passport, and we pay the $2.5 million subscription fee for access. We access a product that they have that they sell it to us and they give us access, but they also, they sell it to other organizations also. They sell it to other public sector clients. They sell it to private clients. And so what we're paying for in the $2.5 million every year is access to the software and whatever version of the software is that they have, their technologists have developed and made readily available for their customers. And so, that's on the Ivalua side. And so on the Accenture side, that $7.5 million, as I mentioned, earlier– so we get– we get the Ivalua software, and it is something that is commercially available, out of the box, pretty generic, and serves procurement and contracting for a very– for a variety of clients, right? So it is– it is gonna be not to the

specificity of New York City procurement laws and rules. And so what Accenture helps us do is customize that software so that it can meet the business needs of our agencies and how we procure and buy, goods and services. You know, for example, if it's a public works, meaning a construction contract, it has to be done by low bid. Other public sector– other private clients don't typically do it that way, right? They do their own process. And so Accenture will help us, um, and I'm using a very sort of like, um, rudimentary example. So they'll help us tailor that software to meet the needs of the city of New York. And then, they will also help us test it before they turn it on. And then after they turn it on, Ivalua and Accenture, they both sort of see how it performs. And then from time to time, whenever you tinker with things, issues pop up, things like bugs. Bugs come up. It's– and so to find out what's causing the bug or causing the software to not perform the way that we expect it to perform, Accenture helps us to do that. And all along the way also our MOCS tech team is part of that, because the idea is that, to– once, you know, some of that upfront work is done with

Accenture, the MOCS tech team is able to troubleshoot and navigate some of those issues.

That is all very helpful. Can I— forgive my ignorance, but– and I recognize this predates your time at MOCS, but was Accenture's role envisioned from the outset of the creation of Passport? Was that kind of from the beginning their role in kind of tailoring and tweaking the system to make it meet our complex needs always kind of incorporated to make this off-the-shelf product work? Is that—

So I'm relying on sort of historical knowledge that has been shared with me. So originally my— so it— so, conceptually there was always envisioned that there would be what they call a systems integrator with the commercially available product, because there was— we— it's just the reality that the City of New York as a client would need a firm to help us do the work to make the software perform for the City of New York and all the agencies. And initially it wasn't Accenture, it was

Got it. Okay, helpful. Citywide contracting– 20 percent of the

city's FY27 prelim budget or $26.3 billion and total of 18,000 contracts is contract spending. How are you thinking about— are you looking at kind of savings opportunities globally across, like, our contracted— our contracts? Is this a helpful— this is obviously not like the MOCS budget savings and efficiencies, but as we look more broadly, has leadership in the administration reached out to solicit your ideas and input on how we might be able to achieve some more ambitious savings goals across contracted spending?

Chair, thank you for the question. It's certainly a question that has come up time to time, understanding there's just so much contracting. You know, $40 billion every single fiscal year, that is a natural place to look for some savings. And you're right, MOCS has traditionally not been in the position to really maybe identify where the potential cost savings could be. We're really trying to make the contracts move and things flow. But and to your– and I'll say this, I– so yes, things cost money in terms of dollars, but things also cost in terms of time. And the delay on contracting has an impact on service delivery and quality of service delivery. So, in some ways when we prioritize on-time

registration and on-time payment, we are trying to reduce the cost of time, right? Which is also in many ways maybe even more important than dollars. But when it comes to the actual let's look for $10 million in like a contract or something like that, we certainly have started some conversations and it is part of like ongoing conversations that, you know, as the city is negotiating and finding its way through this very first budget season that, you know, there'll be more to come.

I appreciate that it's kind of up to each agent— each agency's responsible for their own contracts and evaluating whether there are efficiency opportunities– whether there are opportunities for efficiencies. I'm particularly interested in kind of larger consulting contracts, the, you know, McKinsey [sp?], KPMG-type contracts where we're bringing in these outside vendors, often spending many, many millions of dollars for consulting advice, sometimes on questions as complex as, you know, whether garbage should go in bins, you know, where the Department of Sanitation spent $1.6 million on a contract, or the Department of Education, it was just $760,000, but we spent two

years of the Adams administration waiting for this magical, mysterious 3K analysis from— I think it was Accenture, right? It was Accenture. Not to shit talk, not to criticize Accenture specifically, but, you know, it was a totally useless analysis that I could have written in an afternoon without having looked up anything, just based on what you or I or any semi-informed person knows. So, just interested, is there any broader review of consulting agreements in particular? I'm always interested in what we can bring in-house and how we can ensure that we have the expertise within our city government and not rely on consultants as much. There are times when we need to and we need their expertise, but I think there's often an overreliance in city government. Just wondering if that– it's not necessarily a core MOCS function, but just wondering, is that a conversation that you've been a part of? Is that a review that MOCS could be a part of to help us identify some savings opportunities?

Thank you for the question, Chair. It certainly has come up from time to time. In the City of New York in the— it's just the amount of strategy and, you know, weighing options that is

required of all the organizations. I think from time to time there is this sense that let's get an outside opinion, right? And let's get an outside opinion by an organization we know to be reputable, and they tend to be these larger organizations such as like Deloitte and KPMG and Accenture. And I–
[interposing] And McKinsey.

And McKinsey, yes, yes. And I think also this– under the last administration when there were a fair amount of budget cuts, vacancy reductions that left, I would say that like, you know, you pull at one thing and something else gives, right? And so if you're going to not have the team members to do certain things–
[interposing] You need the consultants.

There's— yeah, you're gonna go outside. And so I think maybe there was like a little bit of that happening. And certainly under the prior– under the last administration, there were some conversations that MOCS was brought into looking at consultant contracts. It's certainly something that cert— in partnership with you, we'd– you know, we

could take a look again at. I do think that there's– it's a– it's a reality that there will be consulting services to the City of New York just based upon the complexity of the work that we do and also our desire to be so innovative and keep up with what's happening in the market.
Totally.
But yes, to do it thoughtfully and in a balanced way and not do it in a wasteful way is something that would welcome working with you on.

Yeah, that's fair. You know, I think, you know, we've seen many examples. I think after the city, state, federal level, after the kind of embarrassment of healthcare.gov in the Obama administration, they made a real effort to kind of create an in-house digital and tech consulting team that was incredibly helpful across the federal government. And I think we're looking for similar innovations here where we can bring in-house capacity that can provide some of that consulting insight and expertise, you know, different— in different administrations, the Mayor's Office of Operations and some of the units under

their purview have had that kind of in-house consultant function much more cost-effectively. And I think often with similar expertise and competencies. So, you know, I agree, it's not to say we're eliminating all consulting contracts or anything like that. But I think that there's been an overreliance on them and an opportunity for savings. So, hope that that's something that we can look at together over the course of this budget process. And I will ask one more question that I imagine is not fully in your wheelhouse, but I'm gonna ask it anyway. I previously chaired the GovOps Committee and, you know, I like backdrop contracts that make it easy for agencies to procure off of, you know, goods and services that we've already completed the procurement, easy for them to access, good for the world. But we sometimes see with backdrop contracts when different agencies procure off of them, they can spend wildly different amounts for similar services, which makes my head want to explode. This was most famously, you know, the example that we always cite, you know, where the security guard contracts in the asylum seeker hotels were H&H and DHS and other agencies were spending radically different sums to the tune of millions of

dollars in differences. If we had all been paying off the DHS rate for security guards, it would have been wildly more cost effective. And when I pushed DCAS on it, because it was a DCAS backdrop contract, they said all we do is the procurement function. It's up to the agencies to negotiate their own rates. I imagine you would have a similar response to me. I don't mean to answer the question for you. But if that's the case, that MOCS isn't looking at the rates that are being paid off backdrop contracts either, like, who should be? How do we ensure that we use this tool of backdrop contracts to make it easy for agencies to access goods and services, but are also getting the best prices across the board? Is that a— is there an opportunity there for savings that with tighter management in a centralized way from City Hall, you know, from the mayor's office broadly, or DCAS where we should be getting where we can achieve some savings across the board?

Chair, I do recall that we've talked about this before, and I would welcome us to do a little bit of a deeper dive into this, especially because, you know, there are– it is like a ready soundbite that, you know, these backdrop

contracts, these master service agreements are sort of– and it is true that they create a lot of efficiencies. You know, you do the procurement up front. You do it for about, you know, 18 to 12 months, and then, you know, once you've got that contract registered to issue, you know, what we call either, you know, the– yeah, the purchase order, the task order, the child contract. It could be very, very quick. And then if we're– if we're just always relying on that efficiency and not looking at maybe the variance in the pricing when you're comparing the sort of the child contractor, the purchase order, the task order, it's sort of– you know, maybe you have some efficiencies one place, but then you're paying more in another place. So I'd welcome looking at this more closely with you.

Like, who should be providing that? Like, who? Whose role is it in city government to be providing that oversight? Do you think that it's the entity that holds the backdrop, like, holds that master contract or backdrop contract that should be evaluating that? Or is that an OMB function or cross-agency?
Potentially cross-agency depending on the contract, but certainly, you know, both of those entities mentioned the procuring agency, and then OMB certainly should be looking.

I wanted to shift briefly to performance evaluation, and I— Council Member Vernikov got at this a little bit earlier as well. You know, we all know that some vendors perform better than others. I could certainly share my list of vendors that perform horribly, but I won't on the record. We can save that for a drink. Agency heads have heard from me. But does MOCS work with agencies to ensure we are setting rigorous performance objectives and evaluation criteria? And then like evaluating that performance, like what are the— when agencies are— when vendors are failing, right, to perform at our collective expectations, you know, when they're being rated unsatisfactory or poor based on their contract evaluation, does MOCS advise that those vendors shouldn't be contracted with? Or is there— are there real-world implications to their poor performance?

Thank you for the question, Chair. The– I'll start this way. I mentioned earlier

when we were talking about just a little bit of the MOCS teams— the General Counsel's Office is broader than just our legal team, and they are ensuring compliance, and they’re ensuring compliance with a number of things, and performance evaluations is one of those things. It is something that– and certainly, you know, with the amount of contracts that are flowing through the system and the amount of performance evaluations that would– that, you know, are within Passport, it tends to be the ones that are more problematic that we spend a little bit of time and energy and focus on. And from– so MOCS does have a role in overseeing particularly the ones where the performance evaluation may be poor or unsatisfactory. And it will not be a surprise when a vendor is— if the agency and the vendor have reached a state in their relationship that the performance evaluation is coming, to the point that a negative— what a negative would be the unsatisfactory or poor. You can imagine that there are other components at play that are signaling that maybe the relationship is not working to the satisfactory of the city's expectations. And so MOCS does have a role in overseeing that, and just sort of recent examples, performance evaluations

sometimes are– the negative ones are coupled with maybe cor— exactly, corrective action plans, cautions that need to be placed on that vendor just to signal to the vendor who has that relationship, the state of the relationship, but then also, because we have the benefit of being in Passport, other agencies are able to leverage that insight and have that information when they may be doing their own procurements and maybe coming across this particular vendor as a potential awardee for their procurements. So yes, MOCS is part of this and we have— we'll be– it's a team within our General Counsel's Office that's called the Vendor Integrity Unit and this is their work.

Great. I remember during the Vendex era that, like, there was a score, right? Do those scores still exist? That, like, you would be scored on your contract and it carried with you and it— you didn't want your Vendex score to go down if you were rated poorly. I was— this— am I making this up? This is my— I mean, it's 20 years back in my brain. It doesn't matter. The– and then just one other question here. I know that we're required to do in most instances kind of lowest bid

to make decisions on contracts, but should we be doing more to favor vendors that have excellent ratings and their performance evaluations as a part of our review and analysis in the procurement process? So, the— just to break it– so the bids are going to be low bid, and so that's going to be, you know, lowest bid is the winner. And then for everything besides public works that are legally required to do as low bid, you can do an RFP, a competitive process that you can factor in a myriad of evaluation criteria. And one of them could be prior performance on other contracts of similar, you know, scope and nature. So there's the ability in the city of New York to do qualitative procurement, and that exists in, you know, RFPs, you know, negotiated acquisitions and a lot of other procurement methods that you can do a qualitative selection and not just low bid. But yes, certainly one of the criteria could be satisfactory or, you know, excellent performance on a prior contract.

Two more topics for me. Firstly, the MOCS Help Desk. So, in FY25, 20 additional positions were added and baselined for the MOCS Help Desk, bringing that total staff to 28

positions. How many employees do you currently have on the Help Desk, and do you think that's an adequate number?

Thank you for the question, Chair. I'm just looking at my notes, if you'll just bear with me. Rather than go from memory, I will commit to following up with you for the overall staffing for the service desk, but I will share for the FY25 additional headcount of the 20, we have– let's see.
You can get back to us.
Okay. All right.

If that's easier. Don't worry about it. We can follow up in writing on that. The– I did want to ask about the kind of backlog of cases. Last year, MOCS indicated that some ticket requests were not getting responded to for two weeks. And just wanted to understand with the additional headcount, were you— and substantial additional headcount– were you able to sh— are you able to share the current number of outstanding ticket requests? Are you able to give insight on how quickly you're able to process those requests now?

Thank you for the question, Chair. Yes. So, rewind to before we got the additional headcount. We had a backlog of about 1,200 tickets, and the 1,200 tickets could have been anything, like an invoice was stuck. I know that a bid is going to close. I wanna get my bid in. So, really impactful tickets potentially, right? And so of the 1,200 backlog tickets, it was taking about two weeks for us to just acknowledge a ticket, because there were so many tickets in the backlog. But I am pleased to share that of the 20 heads that we received, we've done a lot of recruitment, and I want to say we maybe we've seated about 14 of those team members, if not more. And I looked at the numbers earlier this week. So not only are we able to as a ticket comes in, acknowledge receipt within 24 hours, 48 hours. The average time to when we receive a ticket to when we close the ticket is less than four days, because of that additional resourcing that we have capacity.
Closing a ticket in four days as in resolving the issue within four days?
Resolving the issue within four days.
Before it was taking you two weeks to respond?
Yes, before we even touched a ticket.
Pretty great.
Yes.

Congratulations. The– I think that if I have this right, last year testimony indicated that the goal is two days. So we're still working toward it, but four days is a lot better than not responding for two weeks. So that's significant improvement in just the span of one fiscal year. Can I just ask one other related question somewhat more broadly on this? Is like 30 staff, 28 staff on 28 headcount lines, at least, on a Help Desk is a lot of people. Is that indicative of a technology platform that doesn't work as well as it should, that we need so many people for the Help Desk? Like, is there something that we should— it just, it seems to me like that's a big number. I realize we're a big city, and there's 18,000 contracts. The folks at the agencies are doing a lot of work, but it— am I making a improper correlation or— there?
Chair, I think it's something worthwhile to discuss further. And I will sort of like scale out a little bit that the service desk is not just handling tech tickets.
Okay.

So the service desk is providing service to vendors who are– they may have questions about, you know, something. I know I need to re-up my pre-qualified status and like, can you tell me the resources for that? So they're handling other– they're handling other support also. Or it could be that they're onboarding new vendors. And so they're walking them through the process and how to come into the system. And that's not— they're not resolving a tech issue. They're just helping shepherd new vendors in. But it's something that I'm happy to dig in further with you.

Cool. I think we'd also love to dig in further of just if there's any public reporting on this that we could think about. It sounds like things have gotten phenomenally better in a pretty short period of time. So congratulations again. You know, I– as noted, I used to Chair GovOps. I always think a lot about what can go in the MMR and

the PMMR, DMMR, to share information and bring that accountability and transparency. So this could be an area that we could discuss further. Perhaps there's an opportunity. The last topic that I was hoping to ask you about, and then hopefully you'll get some rest is the council discretionary unit that– pilot and kind of innovation that's going on there that Council Member Stevens and Brewer raised earlier. The— so you testified that for the 130 organizations that received grants this year is the first round of the pilot, that they have on average received their funding in about four months, whereas it had previously taken a year. So a 66 percent reduction, that's a big deal. I'm interested in the three-year awards. So, for the non-small— for the not super small neighborhood nonprofits that receive more council discretionary funding and likely also have contracts with the city. Have you seen faster disbursement of funds on those three-year contracts? Any insights or data that you can share there on how that's going?

Sure. Let me– thank you, Chair, for raising this. So let me take a step back and sketch out the multi-year just a bit, and but

also fully acknowledge what Council Member Stevens was saying, that, you know, it's not the panacea, right? It's not the silver bullet. And so, um, the City Council discretionary contract process traditionally City Council members award contracts to community-based organizations or nonprofits within their districts. And there may be situations where there are longstanding relationships and there's– year over year, there's– it's just a– there was not previously before the introduction of a multi-year, the ability to have multi-year terms on those contracts. And so the multiyear was a little bit of an establishment of like a shell, so to speak. And so rather than doing a registration every single year, we did one registration for that current year and then two fiscal years out. So a three-year multi— multiyear, three-year multiyear contract. And what that was able to do is that once we took care of all the processing and did all the steps in Passport to set that shell up, once we went through the entire procurement process and the registration process, that one time, it introduced some efficiencies in year two and year three, because we didn't have to go through that process again if there was a subsequent

follow-up award to that particular organization. And there were instances where there was not an award to that organization, but that's okay too, but the shell was still there in Passport. So that was– that was– we are— 2026 is the third year of that. The first time we did the multi-year. So we did FY24, FY25, FY26. And now we're going to enter into the second of the multi-year process, which is we would do FY27, FY28, FY29. I would say that this concept offers a lot in terms of streamlining and efficiency, but with anything, it's really about the change management. Because I think that there– there would— and I'll— this is— I'm sharing anecdotally. There were some providers who were confused. They benefited from the subsequent two years as part of the multi-year, but it took some time to sort of catch up and have awareness about it. And then now that they're sort of feeling how it can feel without going through the procurement and registration process, and just like upon award, they're leveraging the multi-year. Now we're hitting FY27 and they're like, oh, we got to do this again. And they're thinking that the experience of the prior two fiscal years is what the experience should be for FY27. But all to say, the multi-year is

something that we really tried to introduce some efficiencies and like save some bandwidth on. And Chair, I– you'll indulge me again in the particular sort of where we– where you were hoping that we would go with the multi-year.

Yeah, I mean, I think– well, I have a few somewhat more technical questions on just kind of how things have been working. I will say from the vantage point of like a parochial council member whose allocations change year to year. Some organizations fail to apply year to year. There's been a lot of confusion, and agencies have not done a good job– and I will call out DYCD in particular since most of this is DYCD– in clearly communicating to agencies that this is not a guarantee for multi-year funding.
I see.

And that this is just one year of funding, but they're just trying to make the procurement process– we're trying to make the procurement process work easier and save you a few steps along the way. As noted, not a panacea, but just make it a somewhat easier process. Agency organizations that didn't even apply for funding this

year thought that they were guaranteed a second year of funding with an enhancement because you bake in some increase to that three-year contract. So that's been challenging for us to have to navigate and explain to people like, no, you don't have any money coming, or no, we didn't allocate funding to you, or whatever it may be. So, you know, I'm not— I think that it's well-intentioned, but I think that DYCD and agencies in large, but especially DYCD, need to do a much better job of communicating to vendors what this means and what it doesn't mean. And so I just, I want to flag that very plainly. Not a MOC— I mean, it could be a MOCS thing. It's– but I think more agency, Function– you know, more technically, do you have insight into like how long it's taking to amend these multiyear contracts when amendments are needed? Do— does it— it's not a process that would require re-registration or additional review by the Comptroller’s Office, right, to add a little bit of funding to a three— I mean, or depending, I guess, how much funding is being added– to add a little bit of funding. The council discretionary unit has received feedback that where the shell amount is below the current allocations during enhancement

exercises, that it's been— that I think there's been confusion in that process. So I may— I think there's probably some opportunities for better communication or better coordination with the council discretionary unit on some of these things, but any insight on the contract amendments that you can share?

Chair, I have to be honest that, it's not something I readily have, but I welcome digging in further, because certainly, as you were saying, the communication, it may be something that we can sharpen and make a little bit more crisp. In addition, because we are entering into the second tranche of the multi-year, now would be the time to maybe get some of this ironed out.

Great. Well, we'd be happy to help convene or coordinate or be a part of those conversations. I think, as you've heard from my colleagues, there's a lot of enthusiasm around this, especially the grant component. One other question that I just wanted to ask is if you could provide any more information or insight on the agency subcontracting system. For example, Public Health Solutions at DOHMH or DYCD's YMS system. Do you know how the contracting process is distributed between

in-house review and contracting registration? For those subcontrasting— subcontracting systems?
Chair, I have to be honest, I do not, but it's something that I– we can— I would dig in with you.
We'll follow up with you.
Yeah.
This was a question I was asked to ask, so I asked it.
Okay. All right.
And we'll follow up with you on it. With that, I think we're good. If Molly says we're good. Molly says we're good. You guys are okay? You're good? We're good. Director Yu, thank you very much.
Thank you.
Hope you feel better.
Thank you.

Good afternoon, Chair Restler and members of the Council Committee on Contracts.
I will just thank you in advance, Ms. Kim, for your thoughtful policy reports, which Molly and I have very much enjoyed.
Oh yeah.
Thank you.

No, thank you. Thank you so much, Chair. My name is Gloria Kim. I'm the Director of Policy at the Human Services Council of New York. We're a membership organization representing 180 different human services nonprofits across New York. For too long, nonprofits have incurred substantial costs for service delivery before they are actually paid. So the sector is at a breaking point. The City and its residents ultimately bear the brunt of these problems when highly qualified providers can't afford to take on city contracts, or when those providers

must close programs or go out of business altogether because of the financial strains imposed by the city's late payments. These are not abstract delays. They translate directly into cash flow crises. We recognize that the city has taken steps in recent years to address procurement and payment delays through additional advances. However, this is a short-term fix as the problem remains widespread and systemic. We also asked that Council support Intro 0452, which would introduce a comprehensive new wage requirement system for human services workers aimed at ensuring equitable compensation in line with civil service titles. We see this legislation as an important step toward greater transparency and accountability, as nonprofit human services workers make 30 percent less than their government counterparts performing comparable work. As providers heavily rely on government contracts, those contracts have historically failed to keep pace with inflation, rising costs, and competitive wages. As the human services workforce is disproportionately made up of women and people of color, addressing wage inequities in the sector is a critical step toward broader economic and racial justice in New York City. So this

is an opportunity to move forward from patchwork fixes to systemic solutions, and if we want a result— a resilient, equitable city, we must ensure that the organizations on the front lines are financially stable. So by investing in timely payments, provider stability, and equitable wages for human services workers, the city can strengthen its entire human services ecosystem and in turn better serve millions of New Yorkers. Thank you.
Thank you very much.

Chair Restler and members of the Contracts Committee, it's a pleasure to be here. I'm John MacIntosh from SeaChange, a nonprofit which has been so often asked to summarize the state of procurement that we have built a beta online tool that you can look at at seachangecap.org/contractstat, and see what procurement looks like right now based on publicly available information. I think Director Yu had it about right. Today, in the interest of time, I'll say, there's about 1,600 contracts that are late and 825 amendments in process. And if you do all the math, that's about $1 billion of annualized spend,

which means that every single working day, procurement costs the nonprofits in the city about $4 million. Now, as you know, and I'm the oldest person in the room, so I can say this, things are actually much better than they were 15 years ago. The system that we inherited, in my view, was a monstrous overreaction to the Donald Manes scandal. As you know, Donald killed himself, a bunch of people resigned. There was a big scandal right before the revision of the city basically procurement rules. And so most of what we're stuck with, Vendex, the Procurement Policy Board, the roles of the oversight agencies, all date from 1989. But I do think we've chipped away at it, and my plea to you is that we continue to do that. I mean, through Bloomberg, we got Accelerator, now Passport, super helpful. We got a standard human service contract with de Blasio. We got the Human Services Cost Policy and Procedures Manual. We got the 25 percent advance, which is growing to 50. Organizations are often forced to take out lines of credit just to relieve cash flow issues, only to then have to pay interest. To date, our members have paid over a million dollars in interest on loans they took out while awaiting payment.

Nonprofits typically make requests to add money to their total contract amount due to new expenses they must incur throughout a contract year to operate their programs or shelters. Often these are for increased Indirect Cost Rates (ICRs) - which includes the non-line-item costs associated with running an organization such as payroll fees, and for WEIs, COLAs, insurance costs and prevailing wages. Once DHS and then OMB approve these additional costs for the total contract, the expenses must be added to the individual contract line items in order to invoice against these expenses. This is the FCCR process, which leads to a POCR. Only when the POCR has been approved can an organization invoice for these expenses. Until then, these City-approved additions to a contract sit in limbo even though the nonprofit has expended these costs.

In our jargon, the overall approved budget items are "below the line", and the detailed line-item additions are "above the line". The FCCR is the mechanism to move approved expenses from below line to above line and thus make them invoiceable. For example, one of our members has 15 contracts with DHS, each having below-line items they want to move for a total of $9 million. They worked for 4 months to get just 3 FCCR's approved. This is an extremely long process for our members who cannot afford to have $9m expended but not invoiceable as it sits in limbo.

Last year, we made an incredible headway when the City Council passed Int. 1392 (now Local Law 11-2026), which codifies a predictable and regular payment schedule that is essential to protecting nonprofit shelter providers. We thank the Citty Council for their partnership in this effort. We are excited for the new schedule to take effect starting FY28. However, what remains to be addressed is the backlog of outstanding payments. To accomplish this, we recommend the following: • Implement a bifurcated response to cleaning up the backlog of payments that date back to FY20 while maintaining a consistent payment schedule for FY26 and future fiscal years. • Maintain an adequate staff size in government agency procurement, budget, program departments and MOCS to keep contract registration and issue payments timely. • Establish performance metrics for city agencies on contract registration and payment timeliness that goes above and beyond what is tracked in PASSPort, holding all parties accountable. • Develop contingency plans to maintain services during federal funding uncertainties, particularly given proposed cuts to federal homeless services funding. • Invest in technological enhancements in PASSPort so the system

Finally, we must move to establishing parity in shelter budgets. For the first time in years, the Preliminary Budget makes a more accurate projection of spending on homeless shelters. The Preliminary Budget added $586 million this year and roughly $1 billion in the following years for shelter costs. However, what remains true is that there is a lack of parity across shelter budgets. This imbalance creates significant differences in the level and quality of programming an organization may be able to provide to their clients. New Yorkers experiencing homelessness deserve the same standard of care, regardless of which organization runs the shelter.

In the interest of creating and maintaining high quality facilities and programming at homeless shelters, strong investment must be made in service providers. This manifests as improving the conditions of shelter buildings as well as paying human service workers a living wage. As reported by the Human Services Council, nonprofit workers are paid 30% less than government employees with the same titles. New Yorkers who

dedicate their careers to serving their neighbors should not be subjected to governmentsanctioned poverty wages.

Enhanced shelter standards can also be accomplished through parity in provider contracts. As the cost of living rises throughout the city, state, and country, contracts must rise to match these prices or else leave providers at the risk of footing the cost. Contract standards must be edited to reflect this reality and give providers the resources needed to meet their clients’ needs. This will give all providers an equal ability to meet programming and staff needs and provide the best care possible.

One large step towards establishing parity in shelter contracts would be by passing Int. 452-2026. We are so glad the City Council sees the value and understands the hard work that the thousands of staff at our member organizations provide to New Yorkers experiencing homelessness. We unequivocally believe that they deserve beyond a prevailing wage, and this legislation takes a great step in achieving this. We know that contract-mandated poverty wages are a crucial issue in any organization’s ability to recruit and retain staff. In a survey of HSU’s Adult Shelter Providers, we found that the biggest reason for staff vacancies was because of salary. When organizations lose staff, client-staff ratios increase, and teams get stretched too thin. Ending the crisis of homelessness in NYC requires a steady, consistent, highly trained workforce and establishing prevailing wages for these teams will get us there.

The work of shelter staff and street outreach teams genuinely saves lives. They are more than deserving a prevailing wage.
We look forward to working with the City Council to ensure that this year’s budget delivers for all New Yorkers. If you have any additional questions, please contact me at vleahy@hsunited.org.

New York City Council Committee on Contracts Preliminary Budget Hearing March 24, 2026 Submitted by: Gloria Kim Director of Policy, Research, and Impact Human Services Council of NY Introduction Good afternoon, Chair Restler, and members of the New York City Council Committee on Contracts. My name is Gloria Kim, and I am the Director of Policy, Research, and Impact at the Human Services Council (HSC), a membership organization representing 180 human services providers in New York. HSC serves our membership as a coordinating body, advocate, and intermediary between the human services sector and government. We take on this work so that our members can focus on running their organizations and providing critical direct support to New Yorkers. These are the nonprofits that support our city’s children, seniors, those experiencing homelessness, people with disabilities, individuals who are incarcerated or otherwise involved in the justice system, immigrants, and individuals coping with substance abuse and other mental health and behavioral challenges. We strive to help our members better serve their clients by addressing matters such as government procurement practices, disaster preparedness and recovery, government funding, and public policies that impact the sector. Late Contracting Issues Human services organizations operate on tight margins. Unlike many private-sector contractors, we do not have large reserves or access to flexible capital. Yet we are expected to deliver essential, often life-sustaining services every day, regardless of whether payments from the City arrive on time. When contract payments are delayed by months, as is too often the case, we are forced into an impossible position: either reduce services or take on financial risk to continue operating. Providers have to delay payments, draw on lines of credit, delay vendor payments, and in some instances, make difficult staffing decisions. These are not abstract administrative issues—they directly affect the sector’s ability to provide consistent quality care, maintain experienced staff, and meet the needs of millions of New Yorkers. Compounding this issue are contracting delays and administrative burdens. Although we are grateful to the City Council for legislating advances for human services contracts, these advances are only a short-term solution because nonprofits continue to incur substantial costs for service delivery before they are paid. Reimbursement processes can be complex, inconsistent, and slow, further extending the time between service delivery and payment. These systemic issues create instability across the human services sector. Smaller organizations, in particular, are at risk of closing their doors, reducing access to critical services in the very communities that rely on them most.

Support the #JustPay Campaign and Wage Equity for Human Services Workers We are proud members of the #JustPay campaign, which is a racial equity and gender justice campaign committed to ending the government exploitation of human services workers by demanding sector employees under contract with the New York City and State be paid fair wages for their labor. Each year you hear from providers who are struggling due to the crisis of compounding underfunding of the human services sector as City budgets are balanced on the backs of low-income neighborhoods and BIPOC communities. Government is the predominant funder of human services through government contracts that have resulted in poverty-level wages for human services workers, who are predominantly women and people of color. To address these challenges, we ask that you support Int 0452-2026, which would introduce a a comprehensive new wage requirement system for human services workers, aimed at ensuring equitable compensation in line with civil service titles. Nonprofit workers make 30% less than government workers for the same job. With a City COLA secured for three years, we were able to pivot to fight for systemic policy change to tackle this wage disparity in the long-term. By supporting this legislation, it is a significant step towards ensuring that human services workers receive equitable pay comparable to their City counterparts, recognizing the critical role they play in delivering vital services to our communities. By establishing a clear wage requirement system, this legislation promotes transparency in compensation, ensuring that every worker is paid solely on their qualifications and experience. By guaranteeing just wages and benefits, the sector will continue to attract but, most importantly, retain skilled human services workers, contributing to a more stable and effective workforce that can better serve our communities. According to a budget brief by the Center for New York City Affairs, it would only cost an estimated $965 million to $1.35 billion to provide salary parity for the nonprofit human services workforce. Conclusion Human services providers are proud partners with the City. We are committed to delivering high-quality services and improving outcomes for residents. But we cannot continue to serve effectively under a system that places disproportionate financial strain on the very organizations tasked with caring for our communities. Addressing late payments and contracting inefficiencies is not just a matter of administrative reform—it is essential to ensuring stability, equity, and continuity of care for those who depend on these services. Thank you for your time and your commitment to strengthening the human services sector. Gloria Kim Director of Policy, Research, and Impact Human Services Council of NY kimg@humanservicescouncil.org

Testimony of Legal Services NYC Submitted to the New York City Council Committee on Contracts Preliminary Budget Hearing – March 24, 2026 Greg Klemm, Chief Financial Officer

Introduction Legal Services NYC (LSNYC) is the largest provider of free civil legal services in New York City, serving low-income New Yorkers in every borough. Our staff includes attorneys, paralegals, social workers, and support staff who provide critical legal assistance in housing, immigration, family law, public benefits, and other areas that help stabilize families and communities.

Nearly half of LSNYC’s funding comes from contracts with New York City agencies. These contracts fund essential services that support some of the most vulnerable New Yorkers. However, persistent delays in contract registration, budget approvals, invoice processing, and payments create significant financial strain on our organization and limit our ability to provide services.

Late payments are not just an administrative issue; they are a budget issue. When nonprofit providers are not paid on time, we are forced to borrow on lines of credit to cover payroll and operating expenses while waiting for reimbursement for work already performed. The interest expense incurred from this borrowing reduces the amount of funding available for services and staff. In effect, late payments function as a reduction in funding for nonprofit providers delivering City-funded services.

Late Funding Confirmation and Budget Approval Despite timely contract registration, the Human Resources Administration (HRA) did not approve budget amounts for baseline housing and immigration contracts until just recently. The discretionary contracts are still outstanding. This issue has prevented our timely submission of invoices for expenses incurred and services rendered. For FY25, the AHTP and discretionary contract final, closeout budget modifications are still pending. This represents over $4 million in invoices from the City’s FY25 Fiscal Year that we have not been able to submit.

Although the baseline housing and immigration contracts for FY26 have now been approved, there is a lot of catch-up that still needs to be done. We have the invoices

prepared, but were not able to submit all of them until recently – there is an estimated $22 million owed to us that the City still needs to catch up on. All told, we are still owed at least $26 million for work performed and expenses incurred for which we have not yet been reimbursed. This is nearly 20% of our total annual budget and is not sustainable. Nonprofits do not have the ability to run operating deficits or issue debt like government agencies. When payments are delayed, we must either borrow or delay payments to vendors, both of which increase costs and financial risk.

Invoice Review When submitting invoices or budget modifications, we often face an incredibly onerous and ever-changing submission and review process. This involves detailed line-item reviews that require pages of information and record-keeping to meet extremely detailed and often shifting requirements.

Further, there are often delays in the processing of invoices. At the Office of Civil Justice (OCJ) within HRA, there appears to not be enough staff to keep up with all the work. Our understanding is that there are only two contract managers at the OCJ to administer the contracts for all legal service providers across the City. All these items place a severe strain on our cash position, which is needed to meet payroll and maintain operations. For example, at LSNYC, in 2025, we incurred approximately $475,000 of interest expenses in borrowing on our line of credit. In the first three months of 2026 alone, we have incurred $239K, or nearly $80K per month. Since all resources are finite, this is money that could have been used to hire more staff to serve more New Yorkers. At LSNYC, this translates into about 6 additional attorneys and take on an additional 400 cases to provide services to our clients.

Recommendations Immediate actions needed include: • Approval of remaining FY25 final budget modifications and the FY25 and FY26 discretionary budgets. • Expedited payment for all pending and subsequent invoice submissions for both FY25 and FY26.

To fix this issue going forward, we strongly urge the following: • Increase agency staffing at OCJ. Two contract managers are woefully insufficient to be able to keep up with all of the work and OCJ should have more budget lines for additional staffing.

• Ensure contracts are registered and budgets are approved prior to the start of the FY so that providers can invoice and be paid on a timely basis. • Reimburse organizations for interest expense incurred. LSNYC incurred $475,000 in 2025. Since we have incurred $239,000 already in the first three months of 2026 alone, this number will likely be in the high six-figures this year, which is unsustainable. • Provide transparent, clear instructions on budget submission and processes that do not change and provide an estimated timeline so that cash flow can be projected. Managing liquidity at a mostly government funded social services organization is critical since government funding is almost always cost reimbursement. When NYC funding makes up nearly 50% of revenue, as it does at LSNYC, not being able to estimate the timing of those cash receipts increases the likelihood of sliding into a cash flow emergency.

Conclusion Nonprofit organizations like Legal Services NYC are proud to partner with New York City to provide essential services to low-income New Yorkers. However, the current contracting and payment system forces nonprofits to effectively finance City programs while waiting for payment for work already performed. This is not sustainable and diverts resources away from services and toward interest expense and administrative burden. Improving contract registration, budget approvals, and payment timelines would significantly improve the nonprofit contracting system — it simply requires paying providers on time for services already delivered.
